name: Stellarium
purpose: Planetarium application that renders a photorealistic sky for any location, date and time, including stars, planets, the Moon's phase and position, satellites and atmospheric effects.
journalism_use_case: Verifying or falsifying night-time imagery: set the claimed location and timestamp, and check whether the Moon's phase and position, and the visible star field, match what the photograph or video shows. A waxing Moon in a video claimed to be from a night when the Moon was waning is a hard contradiction.
pros: Night-sky geometry is deterministic astronomy, so a mismatch is a strong falsification rather than a probabilistic hint — among the most reliable verification techniques available
Moon phase and position are visible in a large share of night-time footage and are trivially checkable, making this a high-yield, low-effort test
Visual output is immediately persuasive to an editor: you can show the rendered sky beside the frame
Mature, actively released (v26.3, 2026-09-28) with a large community (10,183 stars) and GPL-2.0 licensing
cons: Light pollution, cloud, lens characteristics and exposure all affect what a camera actually records, so an apparent mismatch can be a photographic artefact rather than a false claim — interpretation requires care
Only applicable to imagery where sky is visible and identifiable, which excludes most footage
Desktop application with a learning curve around setting location, time zone and field of view correctly; a wrong time-zone entry produces a false contradiction
413 open issues and a large feature surface aimed at amateur astronomy rather than forensic use
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 10,183 stars with 413 open issues, release v26.3 (2026-09-28), pushed 2026-11-16, GPL-2.0. Night-sky verification is an established technique in open-source investigation practice, though I verified no specific case through this tool.
assessment: Adopt as a standard check on night-time imagery — it costs minutes and can falsify a claim outright. For your profile the discipline that matters is the same one that bedevils shadow analysis: get the time zone and the UTC offset right before concluding anything, and prefer Moon phase (robust) over faint-star fields (sensitive to exposure and light pollution) as the basis of a published contradiction.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v26.3 (2026-09-28), 10,183 stars, 413 open issues. Regular versioned releases over many years from an established community team.
model_or_data_licence: Bundled star catalogues and satellite TLE data have their own sources and terms; the application fetches updates for some datasets.
licence_restrictions: GPL-2.0 on the application; immaterial for desktop analytical use.
costs: No fee. Runs on an analyst workstation. No paid dependencies.
privacy: Local rendering; the location and time you enter stay on your machine. Optional satellite-orbit data updates fetch from external sources, which discloses nothing about your case.
alternatives: Skyfield for programmatic computation of the same astronomy inside a pipeline
SunCalc for solar rather than stellar geometry
ShadowFinder for daytime shadow-based chronolocation
summary: Planetarium application that renders a photorealistic sky for any location, date and time, including stars, planets…

name: Skyfield
purpose: Python astronomy library computing high-precision positions of the Sun, Moon, planets, stars and Earth-orbiting satellites for any time and observer location, using JPL ephemerides and TLE data.
journalism_use_case: Programmatic verification at scale: check Moon phase and altitude for a hundred claimed timestamps in one pass, or compute whether a specific reconnaissance satellite was overhead at the moment an incident was recorded — a question that recurs in conflict reporting and that cannot be answered by eye.
pros: Satellite-pass computation from TLE data is a distinctive investigative capability: establishing which imaging satellites could have seen an event tells you what imagery might exist and who holds it
High precision with JPL ephemerides, so results are authoritative rather than approximate — appropriate when a published claim rests on them
MIT licensed with outstanding documentation (the project's docs are unusually clear about astronomical pitfalls), which materially reduces the risk of misuse
Pure Python, local, no API keys, so it runs anywhere including an isolated machine
cons: Requires understanding of reference frames, time scales (UTC versus TT versus UT1) and observer geometry; the library is correct but misuse is easy and silent
TLE data for satellite computation must be obtained separately and goes stale quickly, so a pass computed from old elements can be wrong by kilometres
No releases on GitHub (latest tag 1.55), so pinning relies on tags or PyPI
114 open issues on a single-maintainer project; last push 2026-09-29, so cadence is steady but not brisk
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 1,809 stars with 114 open issues, no release objects, latest tag 1.55, last push 2026-09-29, MIT licence. The library is widely used in the astronomy and satellite-tracking communities, which is relevant adjacent credibility.
assessment: Adopt where astronomical checks need to be systematic rather than one-off — and specifically for the satellite-pass question, which is genuinely useful for knowing what imagery to request or FOIA. For your profile the practical caution is TLE freshness: fetch elements close in time to the event you are analysing, and record which element set you used, because a published claim about satellite coverage computed from stale TLEs is indefensible.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-29, no release objects, latest tag 1.55, 1,809 stars, 114 open issues. Six weeks since last push on a mature single-maintainer library with steady long-term development; stable rather than declining.
model_or_data_licence: JPL ephemeris files are US government data; TLE satellite element sets come from sources with their own terms (for example Space-Track registration requirements).
licence_restrictions: None on the code. Satellite TLE sources may require registration and restrict redistribution — check the source you use.
costs: No fee. Ephemeris files are a one-off download of tens to hundreds of MB. Negligible compute.
privacy: Local computation; the only network activity is fetching ephemeris or TLE data, which discloses nothing about your case.
alternatives: Stellarium for visual rather than computational verification
SunCalc or suncalc-py for simple solar geometry
Space-Track or CelesTrak directly for satellite element sets
summary: Python astronomy library computing high-precision positions of the Sun, Moon, planets…

name: suncalc-py
purpose: Python port of suncalc.js computing sun position, sunrise and sunset times and twilight phases, with vectorised operation over arrays of times and locations.
journalism_use_case: Batch solar-geometry checks inside a Python pipeline: given a table of claimed locations and timestamps from social posts or testimony, compute the expected sun azimuth and elevation for each and flag the ones inconsistent with the lighting in the attached imagery.
pros: Vectorised over arrays, so checking thousands of claimed location-time pairs is a single operation — the capability that makes systematic consistency screening possible
Faithful port of a well-tested JavaScript library, so results are comparable with suncalc-based tools including ShadowFinder
MIT licensed, tiny dependency surface, local computation only
Still maintained (pushed 2026-11-02) for a small utility library
cons: No release objects (latest tag v0.1.3), and the pre-1.0 version number signals a small project you should pin by commit
Thin wrapper over simple astronomy: for higher precision or satellite work, Skyfield is the correct tool
Same interpretive caveat as all solar geometry: a mismatch may reflect terrain shadowing, obstruction or a wrong time-zone assumption rather than a false claim
Tiny community (69 stars, 15 open issues) with little documentation beyond the README
feedback: No individual user reports verified — 69 stars means minimal community signal. Documented: no releases, latest tag v0.1.3, last push 2026-11-02, MIT, 15 open issues.
assessment: Integrate it specifically for batch screening, which is where it beats both SunCalc (JavaScript) and ShadowFinder (one case at a time). For your profile the valuable application is triage over a large collection of geotagged or location-claimed posts: compute expected sun position for each, and surface the handful whose lighting is implausible for manual review. Keep Skyfield available for anything where precision matters.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-02, no releases, latest tag v0.1.3, 69 stars, 15 open issues. Recent commits on a small utility; feature-complete for its scope.
alternatives: Skyfield for higher precision and satellite computation
SunCalc (JavaScript) for browser-side checks
ShadowFinder for the full shadow-geometry workflow on a single case
summary: Python port of suncalc.js computing sun position, sunrise and sunset times and twilight phases…

name: meteostat
purpose: Python library providing access to historical weather and climate observations from thousands of stations worldwide, with hourly, daily and monthly aggregation.
journalism_use_case: Weather-based verification and falsification: check whether it was raining, snowing or clear at the claimed place and time of a photograph or video. Wet ground in a clip said to be from a day with no recorded precipitation within 50km is a concrete inconsistency, and dry ground on a day of heavy rain is equally telling.
pros: Weather is an independent, record-based constraint on imagery claims — stronger than any model-based detection and checkable by a reader against the same public records
Global station coverage with a simple Python interface, so a check takes a few lines rather than navigating a meteorological agency's portal
MIT licensed with active maintenance (v2.2.3 released 2026-11-11, same-day push) and a very clean tracker (10 open issues)
Repository renamed from meteostat-python to meteostat (transfer verified by redirect), so the canonical path is current
cons: Station coverage is sparse in exactly the regions where verification is often hardest, and interpolating between distant stations weakens the inference considerably
Local weather can diverge sharply from the nearest station — a convective shower is kilometres wide — so 'no recorded rain' is weaker evidence than it appears
Hourly data availability varies by station and era, so historical checks in some regions return daily aggregates only
Small project (669 stars) dependent on upstream agency data pipelines whose continuity is outside its control
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 669 stars with 10 open issues, release v2.2.3 on 2026-11-11 with same-day push, MIT licence; repository transfer meteostat/meteostat-python → meteostat/meteostat confirmed by API redirect on 2026-11-17.
assessment: Adopt as a routine verification check — it is cheap, independent and based on records a reader can inspect. For your profile the honest framing in published work is to name the station, its distance from the claimed location, and the measurement interval, because that lets the reader judge the inference. Treat a near-station match as corroboration and a mismatch as a question to put to the source rather than a conclusion, unless the distance is small and the weather event large.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-11, latest release v2.2.3 published the same day, 669 stars, 10 open issues. Frequent releases and a near-empty tracker; the project also operates a hosted bulk-data interface.
model_or_data_licence: Underlying observations come from national meteorological services (NOAA, DWD and others) under their own terms; Meteostat documents the sources and their licences.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive. Check the source agency's attribution requirements before republishing observation data as a dataset; most require attribution.
costs: No fee for the library and bulk data. Negligible compute. Meteostat offers a hosted API with paid tiers for higher volume — prices not verified in this survey.
privacy: Bulk data access and local computation disclose nothing about your case. Using the hosted API sends your station and date queries to Meteostat, which weakly indicates your area of interest.
alternatives: wetterdienst for direct access to European national weather services with finer granularity
Open-Meteo for a simpler API including historical reanalysis
National meteorological agency archives directly, which carry more authority for a published claim
summary: Python library providing access to historical weather and climate observations from thousands of stations worldwide, with hourly…
additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure

name: Open-Meteo
purpose: Open-source weather API server providing forecasts and historical reanalysis data from multiple national models, available as a hosted free-for-non-commercial-use service or self-hosted.
journalism_use_case: Historical weather verification using reanalysis data, which gives a value for any coordinate rather than only at station locations — addressing meteostat's sparse-coverage weakness, at the cost of using a model estimate rather than an observation.
pros: Reanalysis coverage means you get a weather estimate for any coordinate, including regions with no nearby station — which is where verification is hardest
Self-hostable under AGPL-3.0, so queries about sensitive coordinates need not go to a third party
Actively developed (1.8.0, 2026-11-03; pushed 2026-11-17) with a substantial community (6,682 stars)
Multiple underlying national models available, so you can compare estimates rather than trusting one
cons: The hosted service is explicitly 'free for non-commercial use' per the repository description, so a commercially operated newsroom using the free tier needs to check its position — and the self-hosted path or a paid tier may be required
Reanalysis is a model estimate, not an observation: it is spatially complete but can be wrong locally, so it is weaker evidence than a nearby station reading and should be described as modelled
AGPL-3.0 network copyleft applies if you modify and expose an instance
Self-hosting requires downloading substantial model data, so it is a real infrastructure commitment rather than a quick deployment; 151 open issues
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 6,682 stars with 151 open issues, release 1.8.0 (2026-11-03), pushed 2026-11-17, AGPL-3.0; the repository describes the hosted service as 'Free Weather Forecast API for non-commercial use', which is the key commercial-use caveat.
assessment: Use it for the coverage gap meteostat leaves, with two decisions made explicitly. First, the commercial-use question on the hosted free tier: verify your position or self-host, because a commercially operated outlet relying on a non-commercial free tier is a licensing exposure. Second, in published work describe reanalysis values as modelled estimates and prefer a station observation where one exists — a reader can check a station reading, and that is worth more than spatial completeness.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 1.8.0 (2026-11-03), 6,682 stars, 151 open issues. Same-day commits and recent releases with a large community and an operating hosted service.
model_or_data_licence: Underlying weather models come from national services (DWD, NOAA, ECMWF and others) with their own terms, several requiring attribution and some restricting commercial redistribution.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0 on the server. The material caveat is the hosted service's stated non-commercial framing — confirm your position before a commercially operated newsroom depends on the free tier. Underlying model data terms vary by source and need checking before republication.
costs: Self-hosting: no software fee but substantial model-data download and storage, plus a server — a real infrastructure commitment (estimate: hundreds of GB and a dedicated VM, depending on which models and history you need). Hosted service free for non-commercial use with paid tiers above that — current prices not verified in this survey.
privacy: Self-hosting keeps coordinate queries private. The hosted API receives the coordinates and dates you query, which indicates your area and period of interest.
alternatives: meteostat for station observations, which are stronger evidence where available
wetterdienst for European national-service data at fine granularity
National agency archives directly for maximum authority in a published claim
blockers: Hosted service is framed as free for non-commercial use — commercial newsrooms must self-host or verify their position
summary: Open-source weather API server providing forecasts and historical reanalysis data from multiple national models…
additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure

name: wetterdienst
purpose: Python library providing a unified interface to open weather and climate data from many national and international providers, including DWD, NOAA, ECCC, IMGW and others, with station metadata and interpolation.
journalism_use_case: Authoritative weather verification from the originating national service rather than an aggregator — which matters when a published claim will be challenged, because citing the national meteorological agency's own record is far stronger than citing a third-party API.
pros: Goes to the national services directly, so your citation is the authoritative record — the decisive advantage for a contested published claim
Unified interface across many providers removes the need to learn each agency's idiosyncratic portal and format, which is otherwise days of work per country
MIT licensed with exceptionally active maintenance (v0.191.0 released 2026-11-17, same-day push)
Includes station metadata and interpolation helpers, so you can report distance-to-station honestly
cons: Very high version number with frequent releases (v0.191.0) suggests a rapidly moving API, so pinning is essential and upgrades may break your code
Provider coverage is strongest for Germany (DWD) and uneven elsewhere, reflecting its origins — check your region before relying on it
63 open issues and a small community (457 stars), so you will read source for unusual providers
Each provider's data model differs underneath the unified interface, so results are not always directly comparable across countries
feedback: No individual user reports verified — 457 stars means limited community signal. Documented: release v0.191.0 on 2026-11-17 with same-day push, 63 open issues, MIT licence. The very high minor version indicates a long sequence of small releases rather than instability per se.
assessment: The right choice when the weather claim matters enough to need the national service's own record — which, for a contested verification, it usually does. For your profile I would use meteostat for quick triage and wetterdienst for anything heading to publication, pinning the version because the release cadence is brisk. Report the station identifier, distance and interval in the story so the reader can verify independently.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v0.191.0 published the same day, 457 stars, 63 open issues. Same-day release and push with a very high release count; unambiguously active, with API churn as the trade-off.
model_or_data_licence: Each national service's data carries its own terms; DWD and NOAA data are generally open with attribution, others vary.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive. Per-provider data terms apply to republication — check the specific agency before publishing a derived dataset.
costs: No fee. Negligible compute; some providers' bulk downloads are large. No paid dependencies.
privacy: Requests go to the national services, which see your station and date queries — a weak indication of your area of interest and generally unproblematic.
alternatives: meteostat for faster, simpler station access
Open-Meteo for reanalysis coverage where no station exists
Direct agency portals for a one-off query
summary: Python library providing a unified interface to open weather and climate data from many national and international providers…

name: sentinelhub-py
purpose: Python library for requesting and processing satellite imagery through Sentinel Hub services, with area-of-interest requests, custom band arithmetic evalscripts and batch processing.
journalism_use_case: Programmatic acquisition of satellite imagery for a specific place and date range — the step before analysis in any before-and-after story about destruction, construction, deforestation or industrial activity. Server-side band arithmetic means you can request a burn or vegetation index directly rather than downloading whole scenes.
pros: Area-of-interest requests with server-side processing avoid downloading gigabyte scenes, which makes iterative satellite investigation practical on an ordinary connection
Evalscript support lets you compute indices (NDVI, NBR, false colour) at request time — the analytical techniques used in environmental and conflict reporting, available in one call
MIT licensed with active maintenance (v3.12.1 released 2026-11-06, same-day push) and a clean tracker (24 open issues)
Gives access to Sentinel-1 radar as well as optical data, which is decisive for cloudy regions and night-time analysis where optical imagery is useless
cons: MATERIAL COST AND LICENCE UNCERTAINTY: the library is free but the service is not, and pricing could NOT be verified in this session — sentinel-hub.com/pricing redirects to planet.com/pricing, which rendered no prices (re-verified 2026-11-17). Treat satellite access as an unpriced dependency requiring a vendor quote
Sentinel Hub is now part of Planet, so the previously available free and research tiers cannot be confirmed as still offered — a continuity risk for any workflow built on them
Your area-of-interest requests go to the vendor, disclosing exactly which locations and dates you are investigating — a serious consideration when the target is a military or industrial site
Processing-unit accounting is complex, so costs are hard to predict before you start; 916 stars means a modest community
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 916 stars with 24 open issues, release v3.12.1 on 2026-11-06 with same-day push, MIT licence. The pricing-page redirect chain was verified twice (session 1 on 2026-11-16 and again on 2026-11-17), and in both cases no prices were retrievable — recorded in sources/evidence/pricing.md.
assessment: Technically the best route to commercial satellite imagery, and the one item in this segment where I cannot give you a cost. Before building anything on it, get a written quote and confirm whether research or non-profit access still exists post-acquisition. For your profile the strategic hedge is to build your analysis on openly licensed Sentinel and Landsat data accessed through pystac or Planetary Computer wherever the story allows, and reserve commercial tasking for cases where nothing else will do — because an unpriced dependency in the middle of an investigation is a planning risk, not just a budget one.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-06, latest release v3.12.1 published the same day, 916 stars, 24 open issues. Current releases under commercial maintenance; the uncertainty is commercial (post-acquisition product direction), not technical.
model_or_data_licence: Imagery licences vary by source: Sentinel data is openly licensed under the Copernicus terms; commercial constellations accessed through the service carry restrictive per-scene terms including limits on redistribution of imagery and sometimes of derived products.
licence_restrictions: Library is unrestricted. The imagery is where the restrictions are, and they matter for publication: confirm redistribution rights for any commercial scene you intend to publish, including whether you may publish a derived index image.
costs: Library free. Service: **not publicly listed — quote required** (verified 2026-11-17: sentinel-hub.com/pricing redirects to planet.com/pricing, which rendered no prices). Historical free and research tiers cannot be confirmed. Budget as an unknown pending a vendor quote; do not plan against any figure from secondary sources.
privacy: Area-of-interest requests disclose the coordinates and dates you are investigating to the vendor. For sensitive sites this is a real exposure — consider whether openly licensed data retrieved from a public archive (less targeted) is sufficient.
alternatives: pystac plus a public STAC catalogue for openly licensed Sentinel/Landsat data at no cost
Microsoft Planetary Computer for free access to a large open-imagery catalogue
Copernicus Open Access Hub / Dataspace directly for Sentinel data
blockers: Service pricing not publicly listed — quote required; post-acquisition availability of free/research tiers unconfirmed
Requests disclose target coordinates and dates to the vendor
summary: Python library for requesting and processing satellite imagery through Sentinel Hub services, with area-of-interest requests…
software_price_note: library free (MIT); Sentinel Hub / Planet service pricing NOT publicly listed — quote required (re-verified 2026-11-17)
additional_costs_note: mandatory paid satellite-imagery service for commercial constellations (quote required); self-hosted compute

name: PySTAC
purpose: Python library for reading, writing and querying SpatioTemporal Asset Catalogs (STAC), the standard for describing and searching geospatial imagery collections.
journalism_use_case: The free route to satellite imagery: search public STAC catalogues (Copernicus, Landsat, Planetary Computer) for every scene covering a location in a date window, then fetch only the bands and area you need — all with no vendor account and no cost.
pros: Opens access to large volumes of openly licensed imagery (Sentinel-1/2, Landsat) at zero cost, which covers a majority of practical before-and-after investigative needs
STAC is now the de facto standard, so one library works across Copernicus, Planetary Computer, USGS and others rather than learning several APIs
Apache-2.0 (licence resolved in this session; GitHub reports NOASSERTION) with very active maintenance (pushed 2026-11-16) under community governance
Cloud-optimised GeoTIFF support means windowed reads of the area of interest only — fast and cheap even over the network
cons: A catalogue client, not an analysis tool: you still need rasterio or GDAL to do anything with the imagery, so it is one component of a pipeline

Resolution is limited to what open programmes provide (Sentinel-2 at 10m, Landsat at 30m), which is insufficient for identifying vehicles, individuals or small structures — commercial imagery remains necessary for those
Release and tag naming is confusing (per-extension release objects alongside a v1.16.0 tag), so pinning takes attention
68 open issues and a spread of related repositories (pystac-client, stac-utils tooling) that you need to navigate to assemble a workflow
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 470 stars with 68 open issues, pushed 2026-11-16, licence resolved to Apache-2.0 by reading the blob (GitHub reports NOASSERTION). STAC's adoption by Copernicus, USGS and Microsoft Planetary Computer is the relevant evidence of its standard status.
assessment: Adopt as your default satellite-imagery access path, with commercial imagery reserved for cases where 10m resolution genuinely will not answer the question. For your profile this is the cost-control decision that matters most in satellite work: most deforestation, flooding, construction-footprint and large-scale destruction stories are answerable at Sentinel-2 resolution for free, and only vehicle- or building-level identification needs a paid scene. Pair with pystac-client for search and rasterio for analysis.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, release objects published per-extension (latest pystac-ext-xarray-assets-v1.0.2, 2026-11-04) with a v1.16.0 tag, 470 stars, 68 open issues. Current commits under stac-utils community governance alongside a widely adopted specification.
licence: Apache-2.0 (licence blob read 2026-11-17; GitHub reports NOASSERTION)
model_or_data_licence: Imagery licences depend entirely on the catalogue: Copernicus Sentinel data is openly licensed with attribution; Landsat is US public domain; commercial catalogues accessed via STAC carry their own restrictive terms.
licence_restrictions: Library permissive. For open programmes the data restrictions are light (attribution), which is the main reason to prefer this path over commercial imagery.
costs: No fee for the library and no fee for open imagery. Cost is bandwidth and storage for the scenes or windows you fetch, plus compute for analysis. Estimate: a before-and-after study of one site is gigabytes, not terabytes.
privacy: Searches and range requests go to the catalogue host (Copernicus, Microsoft, USGS), disclosing your area of interest to that host. Less targeted than a commercial tasking request but not private.
alternatives: sentinelhub-py where higher resolution or server-side processing justifies a paid service
Microsoft Planetary Computer for hosted compute next to the data
Copernicus Dataspace directly for bulk Sentinel downloads
summary: Python library for reading, writing and querying SpatioTemporal Asset Catalogs (STAC)…

name: Microsoft Planetary Computer
purpose: Hosted platform providing a large STAC-indexed catalogue of open environmental and satellite datasets with co-located compute (Hub notebooks) for analysis next to the data.
journalism_use_case: Analysing satellite imagery at scale without downloading it: run a multi-year change-detection analysis over a region in a hosted notebook where the data already sits, which is otherwise infeasible on a newsroom connection.
pros: Co-located compute removes the bandwidth barrier that makes multi-year, multi-scene analysis impractical locally — a genuine capability difference, not just convenience
Very large catalogue of open datasets (Sentinel, Landsat, climate, land cover) indexed with STAC, so acquisition and analysis are in one place
Historically free access to the catalogue and Hub, which makes serious satellite analysis available to newsrooms with no imagery budget
The STAC API is standards-based, so analysis code is portable to other catalogues if the platform changes
cons: Hosted Microsoft platform: your analysis, areas of interest and notebooks sit on Microsoft infrastructure, which is a custody decision — and for investigations into locations in jurisdictions where Microsoft operates commercially, worth thinking about

The GitHub repository is an issues-and-documentation tracker, not the platform code: last push 2024-11-19 with a 2023 release and 80 open issues, so the repository tells you little about the platform's health
Platform continuity and access terms are outside your control, and current access terms and any usage limits were NOT verified in this survey
Requires comfort with notebook-based geospatial Python; not a tool for an analyst without that background
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the GitHub repository is a tracker (210 stars, 80 open issues, release 2023.1.26 from 2023-01-26, last push 2024-11-19) and not the platform itself, so repository-based maintenance assessment is not meaningful for the service. Current access terms were not verified.
assessment: Worth using for the specific case of large-scale, multi-temporal analysis you cannot run locally, treated as a convenience rather than a dependency: keep your analysis code STAC-portable so it can run against Copernicus or elsewhere if access terms change. For your profile the privacy question is the one to settle deliberately — running an investigation's satellite analysis on Microsoft infrastructure discloses the areas and periods of interest, and for a hostile-state subject that may be unacceptable even though the imagery is public.
